title: Collaborative Fund Conversations: Matt Sonsini
author: Morgan Housel & Craig Shapiro
text:
Collaborative Fund Conversations: Matt Sonsini

Oct 13, 2026

SHARE ↓

by

Morgan Housel & Craig Shapiro

The limits of good intentions: Matt Sonsini on philanthropy’s feedback problem, startup term sheets, and learning to be an optimist.

🎙️ Listen on Spotify, Apple, or wherever you get your podcasts.

Matt Sonsini is Managing Partner and co-founder of Ravello Impact, and the former CEO of The Sobrato Organization. Before moving into investing and philanthropy, he spent almost two decades as a corporate lawyer in Silicon Valley, working with startups, venture capitalists, and public companies.

In this conversation, he explains why waiting to give can become its own excuse, why measuring philanthropic impact is harder than measuring investment returns, and what founders sacrifice when they chase the highest valuation. He also revisits the boardroom moment when a CEO quit on the spot and the unlikely IPO that still stands out decades later.

“Well, I guess if you’re Warren Buffett, you have a reasonable shot at compounding capital at a greater rate than the world’s problems are compounding. But for mere mortal investors, I’m personally doubtful that’s the case.”

Key Takeaways:

Giving has its own risk-return spectrum: Local food banks offer immediate, measurable results. Systemic change demands more time, more resources, and a willingness to accept uncertain outcomes. Sonsini approaches those choices as a portfolio, allocating across both.

Good intentions need honest feedback: A business with a bad product hears from the market. A donor can still get a gala and a name on a building without knowing how much good the money did. He also argues that funders, nonprofits, and government need to collaborate more to make their resources count.

A higher valuation can hide a worse deal: Senior liquidation preferences and separate investor approval rights can create conflicts when growth stalls. He urges founders to resist trading away important terms to reach a headline valuation.

Venture’s failures are part of the process: Funding booms draw talent and ideas into new markets. Many companies fail in the correction, but investors cannot know the eventual winners in advance. He sees that experimentation as necessary.

Optimism takes practice: Legal training taught Sonsini to look for downside. Investing taught him that optimism is essential. The best advisers, he says, tell clients which risks matter and which they can stop worrying about.
